item.title: Aesthetics Reading Group (Alexandra King, Simon Fraser University) — Fri Oct 30, 3:00 PM — Jackman Humanities Building
item.description:
The Aesthetics Reading Group is pleased to welcome as guest speaker Alexandra King, associate professor in the Department of Philosophy at Simon Fraser University. Currently, she is thinking through what aesthetic normativity looks like: the shape it takes, its parallels and interactions with other varieties of normativity (like the moral and epistemic), and whether it can be said to exist at all. Within aesthetics, she is also interested in an assortment of issues, including subtlety, high and low art, aesthetic/artistic agency, and applied arts. She also owns, runs, and regularly writes for the aesthetics and philosophy of art blog Aesthetics for Birds, which aims to make concepts and arguments in academic aesthetics accessible to a wide, public audience. Talk Title TBA Talk Abstract TBA
Source: UofT Philosophy

item.title: Civic Meetup #567: Insights from the Tracking (In)justice Project — Tue Nov 3, 7:00 PM — Online: https://link.civictech.ca/zoom / Metro Hall
item.description:
Topic: Insights from the Tracking (In)justice Project
Last year, 61 people died in interactions with the police or in incarceration facilities across the country. Historically, we lacked means for systematically tracking even basic details of the circumstances around these deaths, including rudimentary demographic information (who was killed?), geographic (where were they killed?), as well as investigative outcomes (were any officials held responsible?), and journalistic coverage (has there been any reporting about this)? With a team of researchers spanning Carleton, McGill, Queens, UofT, and UBC, we are developing the Tracking (In)Justice project to systematically and transparently catalogue the circumstances around these deaths, drawing on a mix of sources from government releases, news reporting, and meticulous case-by-case fact checking, tracking these critical details from 2000 onwards.
‎
Speaker: Farhan Samir (in-person)
Farhan Samir is a Natural Sciences and Engineering Rese

item.title: Introduction to 3D Printing for Teens — Thu Nov 5, 4:00 PM — Flemingdon Park
item.description: Learn how 3D printers work and how you can print at the Toronto Public Library’s Digital Innovation Hubs. This class includes hands-on instruction with Prusa Slicer, the software used to prepare your 3D object file for printing on a Prusa MK3S+ 3D printer. Toronto has some wonderful natural spaces tucked between its neighbourhoods, and this walk connects two of them into one longer adventure!
We’ll begin in Scarborough, exploring the **Gatineau Corridor Trail**, with its wildflowers, tall grasses, and green spaces where nature is allowed to grow a little more freely. 🍁 From there, we’ll make our way along some city streets before connecting with another trail system and continuing through the surrounding ravines toward the **Rainbow Tunnel**.
The tunnel is an unusual piece of Toronto history, painted in 1971 by teenager B.C. Johnson as a tribute to his friend Sigred, who died in a car accident. Although the artwork has seen better days, we’ll make a quick stop to see it before continuing toward our final destination.

item.title: Civic Meetup #568: Hack the Count: Turning Window Sensors into Street Safety Evidence — Tue Nov 10, 7:00 PM — Online: https://link.civictech.ca/zoom / Metro Hall
item.description:
Topic: Hack the Count: Turning Window Sensors into Street Safety Evidence
When Ontario removed roughly 700 automated speed enforcement cameras from school and community safety zones in 2025, neighbourhoods lost one of their few sources of hard evidence about speeding. What happens when residents start collecting that evidence themselves?
This talk introduces CIVIC (Community-centred Infrastructures for Visible and Inclusive Cities), an urban living lab in London, Ontario. Residents host low-cost, privacy-by-design Telraam traffic sensors and noise monitors in their own windows. These sensors count cars, cyclists and pedestrians and estimate speeds, all without storing images. Professor Carrie Mitchell will walk through how the network was built, what the data shows, and how residents and city staff are using it to make the case for traffic calming.
